passages.t: ‘The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice’: clouds, fire and light
passages.happening:
Psalm 97 has no heading. It opens with the cry of Book Four: “The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the distant shores be glad” (verse 1).

Then a picture of God's coming, like a great storm. “Clouds and darkness surround Him; righteousness and justice are His throne's foundation” (verse 2). Fire goes before him (verse 3). His lightning lights up the world (verse 4). “The mountains melt like wax at the presence of the LORD” (verse 5).

Everyone sees. “The heavens proclaim His righteousness; all the peoples see His glory” (verse 6). Those who worship idols are put to shame (verse 7). Zion hears and is glad (verse 8).

Then the psalm speaks to God's people. “Hate evil, O you who love the LORD” (verse 10). God guards his faithful ones. “Light shines on the righteous, gladness on the upright in heart” (verse 11). “Rejoice in the LORD, you righteous ones, and praise His holy name” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Clouds, darkness, fire and quaking mountains would remind any Israelite of Mount Sinai, when “the LORD had descended on it in fire” and “the whole mountain quaked violently” (Exodus 19:18).

Israel's neighbours also pictured their gods coming in storms. Baal, the storm god of Canaan, was said to ride the clouds. Psalm 97 uses the same kind of picture, but adds what the others did not: ‘righteousness and justice are His throne's foundation’. A king's throne sat on a raised base. This King's throne rests on what is right.

‘The distant shores’ (verse 1) means the coastlands and islands far to the west, the ends of the world as the first hearers knew it. Even they are called to rejoice.

The book page notes that Book Four sings again and again that the LORD is King. Psalm 97 is one of those psalms.
passages.later:
Hebrews writes, “since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe” (Hebrews 12:28). John writes, “God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5).

Paul echoes verse 10: “Love must be sincere. Detest what is evil; cling to what is good” (Romans 12:9).
passages.hard: Why does a psalm of joy tell people to hate (verse 10)? Look at what it says to hate: evil, not people. To love what is good means to reject what harms it. Being careless about evil would be a failure of love. And the psalm does not make God's people into judges or avengers. It says God guards and rescues. Hatred of evil here is never permission to harm anyone.
passages.asks:
Psalm 97 joins awe and joy. God is fearsome, wrapped in cloud and fire, and that same God is the reason the righteous rejoice. Do you hold both?

Verse 11 is a promise to carry into a dark week: ‘Light shines on the righteous.’ The Hebrew word behind ‘shines’ means ‘sown’, like seed in a field. Light may start small and grow. It is light God gives, and gladness follows.
